canonical_text: Imagine trying to focus when a familiar phone alert sounds. You do not look at the screen. You do not touch the phone. But your attention may still move toward it. A 2022 study tested this idea with 73 university students. They completed 960 rounds of a visual letter task. Some rounds included a notification sound. Others included a neutral comparison sound. The result was clear. People responded more slowly when the notification sound played. Brain-wave recordings also showed a stronger signal during those rounds. The researchers interpreted this as a sign that extra mental control was needed to keep working.

canonical_text: The fourth kind is the Productive Third Place, or PTP. These cafés clearly welcome customer-workers. They may use seats during quiet hours. They may also make the café look active and lively. But not every café wants this model. Coffee Intelligence reported a different choice by The Barn, a Berlin coffee chain. At its Neukölln shop, laptop users occupied more than 70 percent of the seats for long periods. canonical_text: At the end of a taxi ride or a meal, the payment screen asks one small question: How much would you like to tip? But the screen usually gives an answer first. It shows a few suggested percentages. The first choices may be higher than the amount you planned to give. That first number can change the whole decision. A 2014 study looked at more than 13 million credit card taxi payments in New York City. The researchers found a useful natural test. For fares just below $15 and just above $15, the suggested tip menu changed suddenly. The rides were almost the same price, but some passengers saw a different menu.

canonical_text:
At first, the plan sounds strange: lose money now, grow fast, and think about profit later.

But for some startups, user growth can change the product itself. This happens when a business has a network effect.

Think of a service that helps people connect. When more people join, the service can become more useful for each person. Katz and Shapiro explained this idea as “network externalities” in their 1985 work.

Then a powerful circle can begin.

More users create more value. More value attracts more users.

An early lead can build on itself and become a lasting advantage. A late start can also become a bigger problem over time. In such a market, even the product with the best technology may not win.

This is why speed can be a rational choice. Pete Flint of NFX wrote in 2020 that a company with a true network effect may first run at a loss. It tries to reach a large enough network before rivals do. After that, it may be able to move into profit.

canonical_text:
Social media in the UK may soon say “goodnight” at midnight.

The British government shared a new plan on July 15. It is for people aged 16 and 17. The government calls it a digital switch-off period. It would run from midnight to 6 a.m.

During that time, apps under the plan would not open at first. This first setting is called a default. Notifications would stop. Autoplay would stop too. This tool starts the next video on its own.

The apps would also stop feeds that pick posts for each person. These feeds can keep people scrolling for a long time.

The government plans to start it in spring 2027.
